# Lessons and Lashes: The Cane, Monsieur, and Owuo

[Silas Bambil · June 2026]{.meta}

Before anyone comes for me, this is not an attack on teachers. Some of the teachers I had growing up were genuinely amazing and played important roles in my life. Zinkee, my high school mathematics teacher, was one of the reasons I fell in love with mathematics. Sir Bright, my JHS English teacher, believed in me and constantly pushed me to do better. Then there was Madam Benedicta, who drilled composition, comprehension, and summary into us so thoroughly that they became some of my strongest areas in English.

That said, if you attended elementary or junior high school in Ghana in the early 2000s, you probably remember that the cane was never far from reach. I really hated elementary and junior high school. Teachers lashed us for almost everything. You could be beaten for being slow, getting an answer wrong, or even owing school fees, something entirely beyond your control.

The older I get, the more I laugh at some of these experiences. At the time, however, there was nothing funny about them. I sometimes wonder how we managed to concentrate in class when we were constantly worried about who would be lashed next. As good as I was (and still am) at mathematics, I have always struggled with mental arithmetic. I work best with pen and paper. I need time to examine a problem, think through my approach, and work toward a solution.

Yet our mathematics teachers would walk into class on a Monday morning, cane in hand, make everyone stand, and start firing questions at us. If you could not answer within ten seconds, you were getting lashes. At ten or eleven years old, we were beaten like criminals for failing to answer questions that many of us could have solved if given enough time and a piece of paper. I still wonder what those exercises were supposed to achieve. After all, most of us now use calculators for many of those same calculations.

Mental arithmetic was not even our biggest problem. There was also Monsieur, our French teacher. At one point, conjugating French verbs was one of my greatest worries. Monsieur would come to class, write verbs on the board, and expect us to conjugate them on the spot. By now, you can probably guess what happened if you got them wrong.

There was this guy, Ojarere, who really struggled with French. Monsieur Ben Bardis knew this very well, yet he would deliberately write French words on the board and ask Oja to pronounce them. Charley, charley, it was like watching an action movie. 🤣 One day, Chinedu finally had enough and stood up to Monsieur. He could not understand why Monsieur kept asking Oja to pronounce words he struggled with, only to beat him afterward. Chinedu was like, “Woka hyɛ n’ano koraa, ɔbɛka ati. Ɛnti aden na woyɛ saa?”

Our Social Studies teacher in JHS 3 was Sir Mike, whom we affectionately called Owuo. By all standards, he was a good teacher, but he was also incredibly impulsive and quick-tempered. One day, he gave us a quiz on current affairs. There were ten questions, and we had about thirty minutes to answer them. After marking our scripts, he discovered that the highest score in the class was 4.5 out of 10. Owuo was furious. He could not understand how we had performed so poorly. His solution? Three lashes for every incorrect answer.

My boy Coffie scored 2 out of 10. 🤣 To this day, I do not think I have ever felt as sorry for someone as I felt for Coffie that day. He stepped forward and received twenty-four lashes on his buttocks. To make matters worse, he lived in the same neighborhood as Owuo. Owuo reminded him that despite living so close, Coffie had never visited him for academic help, yet he was always outside arguing about football with the neighborhood boys. My man was beaten like a thief.

Then it was my turn. I had answered only four questions correctly, so I stepped forward and received my eighteen lashes. I can tell you firsthand that it was not pleasant. Then came Eunice. 🤣 She had scored zero, which meant she was due for thirty lashes. But the way she slowly got up from her seat and walked to the front of the class made it obvious that nobody was actually going to beat her. Owuo looked her straight in the eye and said, “Mebo wo a, woto bɛsa. Fa w’anim gu aseɛ kɔ tenase.” Whenever Eunice and I get in touch, we still laugh about that incident.

Some of these experiences have become funny with time. Others have not. I barely remember anything useful Atitsobi did as head of the Arts Department, but I vividly remember what he did to me in SHS 2. Kekeli had reported me to him, and I had refused to go and see him because I was preparing for an Economics examination. Shortly before the examination, he beat and humiliated me in front of all the Economics students.

Among those watching was my crush from Business B. Even after all these years, I remember the embarrassment of being beaten in front of everyone. I still resent Atitsobi for what he did. A little patience and understanding on his part could have prevented the entire incident.

What troubles me about these experiences is how normal excessive punishment had become in the schools I attended. We were children. We learned at different speeds and struggled with different subjects. Some of us needed more time to solve mathematical problems, others struggled with French, and some simply did not know enough about current affairs. These were difficulties our teachers were supposed to help us overcome.

Discipline has its place in the classroom, but there is a difference between disciplining a student for misbehaving and punishing one for not knowing something. How was beating Oja supposed to improve his French pronunciation? How were eighteen lashes supposed to improve my knowledge of current affairs?

When I think of Zinkee, I remember how he helped develop my interest in mathematics. When I think of Sir Bright, I remember how much he believed in me. When I think of Madam Benedicta, I remember the English skills she helped me develop. When I think of Atitsobi, I remember being beaten.

Long after their students have left the classroom, what will teachers be remembered for?
